pr_title: demo: security review target — file import with multiple smells

findings.title: Unsafe deserialization with pickle.loads
findings.explanation: The importer deserializes `.pkl`/`.pickle` files with `pickle.loads`. Pickle is code-execution-capable by design: a malicious pickle file can execute arbitrary Python during deserialization. This is especially risky because the module explicitly imports notes from external sources.
findings.suggestion: Do not accept pickle files from untrusted sources. Prefer a safe data format such as JSON, MessagePack without object hooks, or another schema-validated format. If a legacy internal sync format is unavoidable, require strong authentication/integrity protection such as a signature/HMAC over the file and verify it before deserialization, and keep the pickle path inaccessible to user-supplied input.

findings.title: Command injection via subprocess shell=True
findings.explanation: `archive_path` and `dest_dir` are interpolated into a shell command and executed with `shell=True`. If either value is attacker-controlled, shell metacharacters such as `;`, `&&`, backticks, or `$()` can execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of this process.
findings.suggestion: Avoid invoking a shell. Pass arguments as a list, e.g. `subprocess.run(["unzip", "-o", archive_path, "-d", dest_dir], shell=False, check=True)`, or preferably use Python's `zipfile` module with safe path validation. Also validate that paths are expected local paths before use.

findings.title: Uncovered function `import_from_file`
findings.explanation: `import_from_file` is reported as uncovered by tests, so its file import behavior is not currently exercised.
findings.suggestion: Add unit tests for `import_from_file`, covering successful import from a local file and relevant error/edge cases such as missing files or unsupported input formats.

findings.title: Explicitly check for `None` when selecting the target store
findings.explanation: Using `store or NoteStore()` treats any falsy `NoteStore` as absent. If `NoteStore` implements `__len__`/`__bool__`, an empty store passed by the caller may be ignored and imports will be written to a new store instead, making the caller observe no imported notes.
findings.suggestion: Use an explicit `None` check everywhere: `target = store if store is not None else NoteStore()`.

findings.title: Import persists only note text while returning full Note objects
findings.explanation: Imported `Note` objects are returned, but only `n.text` is persisted via `target.add(n.text)`. If `Note` carries identifiers, timestamps, tags, or other fields, the stored data will not match the imported notes, and the returned list may mislead callers about what was actually saved.
findings.suggestion: Provide a store method that persists a complete `Note` object, or clearly convert returned notes to the newly stored records. At minimum, document that imports intentionally preserve only note text.

findings.title: Potential SSRF through unrestricted URL fetching
findings.explanation: `urlopen(url)` fetches an arbitrary caller-provided URL and follows redirects. If an attacker can choose the URL, this can be used for SSRF to reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, loopback-only admin panels, or unsupported schemes handled by urllib.
findings.suggestion: Validate URLs before fetching: allow only `https`, restrict hosts to an allowlist or explicitly block private, loopback, link-local, and metadata IP ranges after DNS resolution, and re-check redirect targets. Consider disabling redirects or implementing a redirect policy. Also enforce response size and content-type limits.

findings.title: Uncovered function `import_from_url`
findings.explanation: `import_from_url` is reported as uncovered by tests, leaving URL-based import behavior unverified.
findings.suggestion: Add unit tests for `import_from_url`, mocking network retrieval to verify successful downloads/imports and failure handling such as HTTP errors or invalid URLs.

findings.title: Uncovered function `extract_archive`
findings.explanation: `extract_archive` is reported as uncovered by tests, so archive extraction paths are not validated.
findings.suggestion: Add unit tests for `extract_archive`, covering successful extraction of a valid archive and error handling for invalid, empty, or unsupported archive files.

findings.title: Shell command construction makes archive extraction fragile
findings.explanation: Building a shell command with interpolated paths makes the archive extraction brittle: paths containing spaces, quotes, or shell metacharacters can fail or be interpreted unexpectedly. This is also harder to test and reason about than passing arguments directly.
findings.suggestion: Avoid the shell and pass arguments as a list, e.g. `subprocess.run(["unzip", "-o", archive_path, "-d", dest_dir], check=True)`, or use Python's `zipfile` module for portability and easier error handling.

findings.title: Unsafe archive extraction may allow path traversal or overwrite
findings.explanation: The archive is extracted wholesale with `unzip -o` into a destination directory without validating member paths. Malicious archives may contain path traversal entries, absolute paths, or symlinks that can cause files to be written outside the intended directory or overwrite files. The `-o` flag makes overwrites non-interactive.
findings.suggestion: Use `zipfile.ZipFile` and validate every member before extraction: reject absolute paths, `..` components, drive prefixes, and symlinks; resolve the final output path and ensure it remains under the destination directory. Avoid unconditional overwrite unless explicitly intended.

findings.title: Uncovered function `import_archive`
findings.explanation: `import_archive` is reported as uncovered by tests, leaving archive import orchestration untested.
findings.suggestion: Add unit tests for `import_archive`, verifying that it extracts an archive and imports contained notes correctly, including cleanup/error behavior when extraction or import fails.

findings.title: Fixed extraction directory can mix stale or concurrent archive contents
findings.explanation: `import_archive` always extracts into `/tmp/notes-import`, never cleans it, and then imports every `*.json` recursively from that directory. Repeated runs can import stale files from previous archives, concurrent imports can interfere with each other, and unrelated JSON files left in the directory may be imported accidentally.
findings.suggestion: Use `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` per import and clean it up automatically. Import only files produced by the current extraction, or require a known manifest/path such as the archive's top-level `notes.json`.

findings.title: Duplicate note parsing and persistence logic across import paths
findings.explanation: The JSON parsing and store insertion flow is duplicated between `import_from_file` and `import_from_url`, and `import_archive` re-enters `import_from_file` for each JSON file. This makes behavior changes, validation, and error handling easy to apply inconsistently across import sources.
findings.suggestion: Extract shared helpers such as `notes_from_json_bytes/raw()` and `add_notes_to_store(notes, store)`. Then file, URL, and archive imports can share validation and persistence behavior.

findings.title: Predictable temporary directory in /tmp
findings.explanation: The importer uses a predictable shared directory under `/tmp` and creates it with `exist_ok=True`. On multi-user systems, another local user or process may pre-create or manipulate this path, leading to race conditions, symlink attacks, data leakage, or contamination between imports.
findings.suggestion: Use `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="notes-import-")` to create a unique private directory for each import, and clean it up after use. If a persistent directory is required, create it with restrictive permissions and fail if it already exists unexpectedly.

summary: The PR has blocking security issues in notes/import_.py: unsafe pickle deserialization and shell-based archive extraction/command execution enable code execution. Additional SSRF, unsafe extraction, quality, and coverage gaps need follow-up.
